The Two Men of Tibet

Graph TheoryParityInvariants
Game: Two men start at the two ends of a mountain range. Can they walk along it and swap places while always staying at exactly the same height?
How to play: Drag the peaks up or down to make a tricky range, then press Start journey and watch them go, turning back when they have to.
Look for the math

The two men can always swap places, though they may have to turn back now and then. The proof turns their journey into a walk on a graph.

Named points

Draw a level line through every corner of the range (Show levels) and mark where those lines cross it. Call the corners and crossings, in order along the range, A, B, …, Z. A position of the two men is an ordered pair of named points at the same height, like (A, Z) at the start. A step takes both men to a neighbouring named point, both going up or both going down, so they stay level.

Counting steps

From (A, Z) there is only one step: both men climb. The same goes for (Z, A). From any other pair there is an even number of steps: 0, 2 or 4. For example, a man on a slope can go up or down, and a man on a peak can only go down, but either way. (The men may not walk side by side: that keeps the count even where they meet.)

The handshake argument

Start at (A, Z) and keep walking along new edges for as long as you can. Every pair you pass through in the middle of the walk uses up two of its edges, one to arrive and one to leave, so you can only get stuck at a pair with an odd number of edges. By the handshake lemma that pair must be (Z, A): the men have swapped. The logic test checked the edge counts on thousands of random ranges, and the walk the page shows is the shortest one in this graph.

Make a low hill near one man and a high peak near the other. How many times must someone turn back?
